## composables

Vue 3 composables providing reusable logic for the inksprite application.

## Composables Overview

### AI

- **useAIChat** - A chat turn: context, request, tool calls, and streaming into a message; one per chat, so a reply outlives the view showing it; `askInThread` asks its model something at the end of the conversation in place of a turn (a summary)
- **useChatActivity** - Which chats the model is working in, app-wide, and word when it stops
- **useChatTabs** - A project's chat tabs: open, showing, previews, the history closing goes back through, and unread chats
- **useChatPlaces** - Where the writer was in each chat they left, for its tab coming back
- **useAIConfig** - AI configuration (provider + model)
- **useConnections** - The AI connections the writer has: which are theirs, how each answered last, and adding, checking and removing one
- **useSignIn** - Connecting an account by signing in to a service that makes the app a key: OpenRouter and NanoGPT
- **useWebSearch** - Web search as the settings set it up: the service in use and whether a page is kept without asking, and each service's key
- **useModelLists** - The models each provider serves, app-wide: asked for on Connect or Refresh, never as an address is typed
- **useExplore** - Exploring a folder, a document or the project for the model, on the chat's model: asked first with its size, then the job
- **useProfiles** - The chat profiles: how a chat is run, built-in and saved
- **useSkills** - The writer's own skills: the library, a file kept as it is written (`createSkill`, `writeSkill`), and why one can't be used (`problemOf`)
- **useMcpServers** - The writer's MCP servers: adding one after a look at what it offers, listing it again, its profiles and the tools always allowed
- **useToolApprovals** - The calls of a server's tools waiting on the writer to allow them
- **usePrompts** - Legacy. The prompt library the profiles replaced; read by cleanup alone

### Data

- **useProjects** - Every project, and creating, importing, opening and deleting them
- **useDocuments** - A story's document tree, shaped for the tree UI, and the editor's tabs
- **useChats** - Chat session management
- **useChatSettings** - One chat's settings and profile, started or not
- **useChatPresets** - Giving every chat the model it runs on, so a pick on its profile, or a preset changed or deleted, never moves it
- **useToolChoices** - Giving every profile and chat, once, the web, Python and MCP servers as switches of its own, from the lists that said before
- **useBackup** - Whole-database export and restore, and single chats, projects and settings as files
- **useExport** - A project, a folder or a document handed out as it would be published, a zip of it where it is more than one file
- **usePrint** - A document printed, or saved as a PDF, in the editor's styles, on Command-P and Export as PDF…
- **useTrash** - The trash: what a project's holds of its documents and chats, and the projects in it, to restore or delete for good
- **useVersions** - A text document's versions, listed, compared with the text now, restored, named and kept; and the Versions dialog's state
- **useNarration** - A project read aloud: its voices and hints, a document's speakers, and the readings
- **useComments** - The writer's comments in a project, by document, kept up as they are typed; going to one, and resolving it
- **useSpeech** - Something read aloud then and there, a line at a time: a chat message. One thing at a time, app-wide
- **useSpeechServer** - What documents are read aloud through: a project's connection and model, as a request needs them, and the model's voices

### UI

- **useEditor** - The open documents: an editor state each, and their projection into the store
- **useToast** - Toast notification system
- **useScreenSize** - Breakpoint-aware screen size
- **useKeyboardCover** - How much of an element the on-screen keyboard covers
- **useMessageField** - The chat's message field, fitted to its draft
- **useLinkMenu** - The documents `[[` lists in the message field, folders among them, and `@`, which attaches the one picked
- **useCommandMenu** - The menu of commands a slash at the start of a line opens in the message field
- **useJumpToBottom** - When to offer the way back to the end of a long chat: far from it, and heading for it
- **useNearScreen** - Which rows of a long list are on the screen or close to it, so only those are drawn in full
- **useNearTurns** - Which of a chat's turns are in the page: those near the screen, the newest two, and any with an editor open; plus the state a turn keeps while it is away
- **useSettingsPanel** - Opening the settings, on a section and a part of it, from anywhere in the writer
- **useCardLibraryPanel** - Opening the card library, to browse or to pick a card for a folder, from anywhere in the writer
- **useSidebarTab** - Showing a sidebar list, such as the narration, from anywhere in the writer
- **useEditorRequest** - Showing the editor, having opened a tab in it, from anywhere in the writer
- **useChatRequest** - Showing a chat in the project it is in, once that project is open, from anywhere in the writer
- **useFocusMode** - Focus mode: the document alone, full screen, in and out on Option-Command-F
- **useTopmostEscape** - Escape closes the dialog on top, and only that one
- **useCopyLink** - Copy a link to a document, its path the address the tools take, to the clipboard
- **useReveal** - Show a document where it is on disk, in the desktop app's file manager
- **useDocumentLinks** - Links between a project's documents: one opens the document in a tab,
  and the link field makes one from a path or a name
- **usePictures** - What a picture's path in a document is (its own, a file document, or the
  web), and opening one
- **usePictureViewer** - The picture shown at its own size over the whole window, from anywhere
- **usePlainText** - Turn a document plain or back, with an undo when that rewrote its text
- **useLongPress** - A finger held still on something, for what a right-click opens elsewhere
- **useTreeDrop** - A document dragged onto a folder's row goes into the folder, and a shut
  one held over opens; the folder a drop would go into, shown whole
- **useTreeHistory** - Command-Z and Shift-Command-Z for what the writer does in the outline:
  making, renaming, moving and deleting documents
- **useFindKey** - Command-F (Control-F off a Mac) opens the find of the panel the writer is in
- **useLastOpened** - Keeps which project the writer was last in, which the app opens on
- **useProjectActions** - What can be done to a project, as menu items, the open one or another
- **useHoverSubmenus** - A TieredMenu's submenus opening on hover, once the pointer rests
- **useProjectSearch** - The search across a project: what is looked for, what it finds, going to a match, and Command-Shift-F
- **useChatFind** - Finding in a chat, most of which is not in the page: counted in the messages, gone to and highlighted in the page
- **useTheme** - The page in the writer's theme, following the system's while that is the one chosen (`useSystemSettings.js`)
- **useUpdates** - In the desktop app, an update downloaded as soon as there is one, and a toast to restart into it; in a browser, a toast to reload into a new build
- **useSaveBeforeClosing** - In the desktop app, edits saved before the window closes or the app quits
- **useSettingsFile** - In the desktop app, the settings file a script left in the data folder, imported as the app opens

## Patterns

All composables follow Vue 3 Composition API patterns:

- Return reactive refs and computed properties
- Provide methods for data manipulation
- Handle side effects with watchers
- Clean up resources in onUnmounted

### Examples

```javascript
// A story's tree
import { useDocuments } from '@/composables/useDocuments'

const documents = useDocuments(storyId)
await documents.init()

const chapters = documents.childrenOf(`manuscript_${storyId}`)
documents.rename(chapters[0].id, 'The Long Road')
documents.setContent(chapters[0].id, '# The Long Road')
```

## composables/useAIChat

Composable for AI-powered chat conversations. Handles streaming
chat responses, context building from story content, and integration with chat messages.
This is the primary interface for the chat assistant feature.

One instance per chat, as `useChats` keeps one per project: a reply belongs
to its chat, not to the view showing it, so a writer who goes to another
chat and comes back finds it still working, with its progress and its stop.

### Examples

```javascript
const { sendMessage, isGenerating, stopGeneration } = useAIChat(storyId, chatId)

// Send a message and get AI response
await sendMessage('Help me develop this character')
```

## TurnActivity

What the turn being generated is doing right now. `calling` is the model
writing the round's calls, and `running` is those tools at work. `waiting` is a request out with nothing back yet — after a
tool result that can be a long time, while the model takes in what the tool
returned. `thinking` and `writing` are the model streaming one or the other.

Live only, and never stored: a page reloaded mid-turn has no turn running,
and nothing left over should say it has.

Type: [Object][2597]

### Properties

- `messageId` **[string][2594]** The message the turn is writing into
- `phase` **(`"calling"` | `"running"` | `"waiting"` | `"thinking"` | `"writing"`)**&#x20;
- `since` **[number][2595]?** When a wait began, for saying how long it has been
- `progress` **[string][2594]?** While they run: how far a long one has got,
  as it said ("3 of 7 requests")

## resolveSystemPrompt

The system prompt for this chat: its own, once the writer has changed it
here, and its profile's otherwise.

Read fresh each turn, so an edit in the settings lands on the next
request — the way the profile's parameters do. The profile itself never enters into it: switching models
shouldn't change what the assistant was told to be.

The prompt replaces the built-in outright, so it owns any tool and oracle
instructions it still wants followed, and an empty one means "send no
instructions" rather than "use the default". Only a chat with no prompt,
or one whose prompt has since been deleted, falls back to the built-in
its story starts chats on.

The chat's roleplay prompt, a card's for a chat on one, goes after it. See
`withOriginal`.

Returns **[Promise][2599]<[string][2594]>**&#x20;

very prompt it is about to use.

so three rolls of the same die are three rolls and not a loop.

Returns **[Promise][2599]\<T>**&#x20;

## consult

Run another inference over this same conversation under a different system
prompt, and hand back what it said.

This is how a skill reaches a model — see ai/skills/index.js. Its request
is its own, stopped by the signal of the call it was made from, so a skill
runs out of time or stops with the turn without touching anything else.
Nothing streams: what a skill says is for the model that asked, not for
the player.

A skill that names tools gets a small loop of its own, over the same
executor the turn loop uses, so a tool behaves identically whichever role
reached for it. What it may reach for comes from the skill and not from
this chat's tool switches: those say what the assistant the writer is
talking to may do, and a skill is not that assistant. Its calls and their
results live in this local array — nothing is streamed, stored, or
replayed on a later turn, and the caller sees only the sentences at the
end.

The request differs from the turn's own only in the system message, which
is position zero — so the two share no cached prefix and each keeps a cache
line of its own. Cheaper than it sounds turn to turn, since each hits its
own entry and pays full price only on what is new. But it means a skill
called _occasionally_ costs more per call than one called every turn: let
its entry age past the cache TTL and the next call rewrites the whole
conversation. Cadence is not the saving it looks like.

### Parameters

- `systemPrompt` **[string][2594]** The role to run as
- `toolNames` **[Array][2596]<[string][2594]>?** Tools the skill is asking for, by name (optional, default `[]`)
- `options` **[Object][2597]?** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `options.depth` **[number][2595]?** How many skills deep this consultation
    is. The turn is 0 and each skill it reaches through adds one; a skill
    among the names is offered only while there is depth left for it. The
    loop sets it, not the skill: a skill that named its own depth could
    claim to be shallower than it is.
  - `options.before` **[string][2594]?** Read the conversation as it stood before
    this message. Set by a caller whose consultation is itself a message in
    the chat, so it neither reads itself nor, asked again later, reads a
    conversation that has moved on without it.
  - `options.past` **[number][2595]?** With `before`: read this many messages
    past it as well. Compaction's, whose summary sits above the turns that
    were kept and read them all the same.
  - `options.edits` **[Array][2596]\<DocumentEdit>?** The turn's record of what its
    tools changed, for the skill's own writes to join
  - `options.signal` **AbortSignal?** Stops it. Set by whoever runs the
    work it is part of, not by the skill.

<!---->

- Throws **any** The signal's reason, once stopped

Returns **[Promise][2599]<[string][2594]>** What it said, or '' if it said nothing usable

## IN_THREAD_ROUNDS

How many times a request asked in the thread is made before it has to have answered.

Type: [number][2595]

## NO_TOOLS_NOW

What a call gets back while something is asked in the thread: no tool runs.

## askInThread

Ask the chat's own model something at the end of the conversation as it
reads it, in place of a turn, and hand back what it said.

The request is the turn's own with one message after it: the same system
prompt, the same tools, and the conversation with every call it kept and
every document the writer attached. So the model answers from everything
the conversation holds, where a transcript has only what was said, and
the request shares the turn's cached prefix: a server at home goes on
from what it has already read, and a hosted one bills it as cached. All
but the last turn, which sheds its project block as on any next turn.

The tools are offered because they are part of that prefix, and none is
run: a call is answered that there are none, and the question asked again.
The author's note stays out. It is standing instructions for a turn (how
long a reply runs, whose lines to leave alone), and this is not one.

Nothing is stored: the instruction and what was said to it are the
caller's to keep or not.

### Parameters

- `instruction` **[string][2594]** What is asked, as the writer's last word
- `options` **[Object][2597]?** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `options.before` **[string][2594]?** Read the conversation as it stood
    before this message, as `consult` does
  - `options.past` **[number][2595]?** With `before`: this many messages past it
  - `options.signal` **AbortSignal?** Stops it

<!---->

- Throws **any** The signal's reason, once stopped

Returns **[Promise][2599]<[string][2594]>** What it said, or '' if it said nothing usable

## executeToolCalls

Execute tool calls concurrently and return their API result messages
in input order.

Including a skill and an ordinary tool called together. A call made in the
same step as `director` was chosen without the direction, and one of them —
the oracle, asked a question the Director is asking too — can come back
disagreeing with it. Holding those back cost every other call in the step a
round trip it did not need, for a rule the prompt can state: ask the
Director first, and don't re-ask what it tells you it already asked.

Skills run as many at a time as the chat's connection takes requests
(ai/gate.js): on a server at home, one after another, so each keeps the
server's slot, and the prompt it holds, through all its rounds rather
than taking turns with the others request by request.

### Parameters

- `toolCalls` **[Array][2596]\<ToolCall>**&#x20;
- `depth` **[number][2595]** How many skills deep these calls are being made.
  The turn's own are 0; a skill reached from here consults one deeper.
- `edits` **([Array][2596]\<DocumentEdit> | [undefined][2602])** The turn's record of what its tools
  changed, for a writing tool to add to. A skill's calls add to the same
  record: they are the turn's changes too.
- `signal` **AbortSignal** The work's, which stops the calls with it

Returns **[Promise][2599]<[Array][2596]\<ApiMessage>>**&#x20;

## runToolCall

Run one tool call, and when it is a skill, keep what the skill did on the
way to its answer beside its result: what it thought, and the tools it
called. The turn shows a consultation as a block of its own, and a block
that showed only the answer would leave out the part worth reading when
the answer came out strange. Kept as `_consultation`, a note to ourselves
that never reaches the wire, like `_document`.

No documentId: nothing is scoped to "the document the writer is looking
at" any more. A tool that acts on a document is told which one.

### Parameters

- `toolCall` **ToolCall**&#x20;
- `depth` **[number][2595]** How many skills deep the call is made. The turn's
  own are 0; a skill reached from here consults one deeper.
- `edits` **([Array][2596]\<DocumentEdit> | [undefined][2602])** The turn's record of what its tools changed
- `signal` **AbortSignal** The work's
- `stream` (optional, default `{}`)

Returns **[Promise][2599]\<ApiMessage>**&#x20;

## handOverReply

Run a round in which the model handed its reply to a skill.

The round's other calls first, since what they do — a document written, a
question answered — is there for the skill to read. Then the skill, its
words streamed into the message as the reply and its thinking after the
turn's own. What the model wrote before handing over is its working, not
the reply, so it goes in with the thinking, folded.

One voice writes the reply: a second skill handed it in the same round is
answered with an error and not run.

A skill that writes something has written the reply, and its result says
so rather than holding the text a second time: no round follows to read
it, and the message's content is the one copy. One that writes nothing, or
fails, gives the turn back as it was — its words, its thinking — and the
model reads the error in the next round, as it would any tool's.

### Parameters

- `toolCalls` **[Array][2596]\<ToolCall>** The round's calls, one of them handing over
- `messageId` **[string][2594]** The assistant message being written
- `state` **[StreamingState][129]** The turn's streaming state
- `edits` **[Array][2596]\<DocumentEdit>** The turn's record of what its tools changed
- `signal` **AbortSignal** The turn's

Returns **[Promise][2599]<{results: [Array][2596]\<ApiMessage>, wrote: [boolean][2600]}>** The round's
results in call order, and whether the reply was written

## answered

Type: [Map][2598]\<ToolCall, ApiMessage>

been switched off since the turn began. Switching it off forgets every

## runCompletionLoop

Run the completion loop, handling tool calls until done.

Produces an apiTrajectory: the per-iteration assistant deltas (with any
tool_calls), followed by tool result messages, followed by the final
assistant text. Each assistant entry carries only the content streamed
during that iteration — not cumulative content — which is the wire format
the turn itself continues in. Stored afterwards as the record of what the
turn called; a later request sends the turn's words as its content and
replays only the calls worth it. See ai/context/build.js.

state.content stays cumulative because that's what the chat UI renders.

A round that calls a skill whose answer is the reply hands the turn to it,
and the turn ends on what it writes. See handOverReply.

A turn that has made the rounds the writer allows it (`maxToolRounds`), or
that keeps making the same calls and getting the same answers, is told so
and asked once more with the tools switched off, so it ends by saying
where it got to rather than mid-work.

### Parameters

- `params` **[Object][2597]**&#x20;
  - `params.messages` **[Array][2596]** Initial messages
  - `params.messageId` **[string][2594]** Assistant message ID for streaming
  - `params.turnMetadata` **[Object][2597]?** Metadata already on the message, carried
    through the mid-turn writes because updateMessage replaces metadata whole (optional, default `{}`)
  - `params.signal` **AbortSignal** The turn's. Once it is aborted the
    loop writes nothing more and throws its reason.
  - `params.profile` &#x20;
  - `params.tools` &#x20;

## insertMessage

Write a turn into the chat without asking for one back.

Two things the writer can only do by hand: say something the model is not
meant to answer yet — three oracles, a note, the next beat — and write the
assistant's turn themselves, which is how a voice gets corrected or a scene
gets opened the way it needs to open.

As the writer, this is `sendMessage` without the reply: the same submission,
so a pushed turn can still carry commands and they still run. As the
assistant it is the text and nothing else — no commands, because a slash in
narration is a slash, and no title, because inserting is the one thing here
that promises not to call a model.

### Parameters

- `text` **[string][2594]** What to write
- `role` **(`"user"` | `"assistant"`)?** Whose turn it is (optional, default `'user'`)

Returns **[Promise][2599]<(Message | null)>** The last message written, or null if there
was nothing to write

## regenerateMessage

Ask a message again.

The answer it has is kept, to be turned back to — see beginAlternate —
and everything after it goes, since it was written to that answer. What
the turns from here on did to the project goes with them, so the retry
starts from where the writer was. What cannot be undone is said, not
forced.

Returns **[Promise][2599]<(Message | null)>** The message, answered again, or null

## rerunCommand

Ask a command's question again.

Here rather than in the component because a command that consults needs a
model, and this is where the model is. See useChatCommands.

### Parameters

- `messageId` **[string][2594]** A message carrying a command
- `index` **([number][2595] | null)?** Which segment, on a turn the writer took (optional, default `null`)

Returns **[Promise][2599]<(Message | null)>**&#x20;

## editCommand

Change what a message says, or what a command in it asked.

Held the same way `rerunCommand` is held, because it is sometimes the same
thing: an edit that changes which command this is, or one to a command
whose answer is its question, runs it again — and running it again may
reach a model. See useChatCommands.

Most edits reach nothing, though — a typo, a line of prose, a roll
fudged — and none of those should wait on a reply that is being written.
So while one is, the edit goes ahead without a model to consult, and only
one that needs it is refused — along with any edit to the last message,
which is the one being written and would be written straight over.

### Parameters

- `messageId` **[string][2594]** A message carrying a command
- `index` **([number][2595] | null)** Which piece, or null for the whole turn
- `text` **[string][2594]** The turn as the writer has now written it

Returns **[Promise][2599]<(Message | null)>**&#x20;

Stop the work under way: its request, its tools, its skills. What a turn

the question asked again — is the only thing touching it.

## useAIConfig

Composable for managing AI configuration: the connections, and each
model's settings.

A chat runs on the model it first answered on, or has been moved to since;
one that hasn't answered, on its profile's (`presetFor`). A model's
settings are a preset, one to a connection and model, made the first time
the writer changes one and holding only the changes (`runOn`). There is no
model for the app: each profile has one its chats start on (see
composables/useProfiles.js).

##

Type: const

## delta

Type: `"function"`

## ReasoningDetail

Reasoning detail entry from OpenRouter extended thinking.

The fields below are the ones we know by name; the shape varies by reasoning
type — a summarized or encrypted block carries an opaque payload instead of
readable text. Anything a provider sends is passed through untouched, since
a block that has lost a field it was signed with is a block the provider
will reject when the turn continues.

Type: [Object][2597]

### Properties

- `type` **[string][2594]** Type of reasoning (e.g., 'reasoning.text')
- `text` **[string][2594]?** Reasoning text content
- `signature` **[string][2594]?** Cryptographic signature for continuation
- `data` **[string][2594]?** Encrypted reasoning, for a block the provider doesn't show
- `format` **[string][2594]?** Format identifier (e.g., 'anthropic-claude-v1')
- `index` **[number][2595]** Index in the reasoning chain

## accumulateReasoningDetails

Accumulate reasoning_details from streaming deltas, merged by index.

Only `text` arrives in pieces. Everything else — signatures, formats,
encrypted payloads, whatever a provider names its own fields — comes whole,
so the later value wins and unrecognised fields ride along. Naming the
fields we keep would quietly gut any block that isn't plain text, and the
failure shows up later, mid-tool-loop, as a rejected continuation.

### Parameters

- `accumulated` **[Array][2596]<[ReasoningDetail][263]>** Array of accumulated reasoning details
- `deltas` **[Array][2596]<[ReasoningDetail][263]>** Deltas to merge

## listModelProviders

The upstream providers that serve one model on OpenRouter, so a picker for
that model can offer them and not the hundred that don't. Public, like the
directory.

OpenRouter lists endpoints, not providers: one provider can serve a model
several ways (`baseten/fp8`, `baseten/fast`), and the part of the tag before
the slash is the provider's slug, the one routing takes. An empty list is
not "nobody serves it" — a router model like `openrouter/auto` has no
endpoints of its own — so the caller decides what empty means.

## explainFailure

Say what a provider's refusal actually means, when it means the reasoning.

Two ways a request gets refused over thinking, and they need different
advice. Extended thinking blocks come back signed, and a provider refuses a
continuation whose signature it cannot verify. Separately, a model whose
thinking is a switch rather than a dial refuses an effort level outright —
DeepSeek answers "thinking mode openai_effort is not supported" — and that
one fails on the first request of the turn, before any reasoning has been
echoed anywhere.

From the writer's side both are a turn that died quoting a field they have
never heard of, so name it and say what to change. Also warns, since the
message the provider sent is worth having in full.

The third is routing. A connection's policy — the privacy and precision
floor it has by default — can exclude every endpoint that serves a model,
and so can the providers a model is limited to, when none of them serves
it any more. OpenRouter answers with a 404 that names the filter and
nothing else. The writer never set the floor, and may have set the list
long ago, so say where both live. A chat says it in its own words
(`describeFailure`); this is for everywhere else a reply can fail.

### Parameters

- `reported` **unknown** What the provider said
- `$1` **[Object][2597]**&#x20;
  - `$1.sentReasoning` &#x20;
  - `$1.askedForEffort` &#x20;
  - `$1.routingStep` &#x20;

Returns **[string][2594]**&#x20;

## composables/useBackup

Whole-database backup and restore — the manual recovery path —
and single chats and settings files in the same envelope. A project, a
folder or a document handed out to be used elsewhere is an export
(`composables/useExport.js`), and nothing here.

A backup is everything: it flushes anything the sync store is still
holding, reads every table, adds the settings kept outside the database
(see `BackedUpSettings`), and hands back a zip: the rows as JSON, each
file's bytes as they are (`utils/backupArchive.js`). What holds no files,
a chat or a settings file, is still one JSON file. Import takes either,
and the JSON backups written before. On a device that syncs, the files
whose bytes are still on the sync server are fetched first
(`cloud/onDemand.js`), and a backup that can't fetch them stops and says
so rather than leave them out.

A backup taken back either replaces the database wholesale, every table
cleared and filled from the file, or gives some of its projects and cards
to be added beside what is here (`addFromBackup`), under new ids. Nothing
merges one history of a project into another, because reconciling two
divergent histories of the same story is guesswork and a recovery tool
should not guess.

Pinia stores cache rows in memory, so a caller that restores must reload the
page afterwards. `restoreBackup` deliberately does not reload on its own —
that keeps it testable and lets the caller show a toast first.

A chat exported on its own is read back by `readChatFile` and handed to
`useChats().importChat`, which adds it to a story through the stores. That
path replaces nothing, so it needs no reload.

`readChatFile` also takes a chat exported from SillyTavern, which is not a
backup of anything but arrives by the same door: the writer has a chat in a
file and wants it in the project. See `cards/transcript.js`.

A project added from a backup carries its tree, the bytes of its files, its
chats with their messages, and the writer's own profiles they run on, and
leaves its trash, its documents' versions and its jobs behind: what a
finished job made is already in the tree, and one still running is work
on that database, not the project's. `importProject` adds it under new
ids, so it never replaces anything.

A settings file carries the writer's setup without their projects: the
connections, presets, profiles, servers and skills they picked, and the
settings kept outside the database (`utils/settingsTree.js` is how they
pick). It is read back by `readDataFile`, which takes a whole backup too,
and merged into the setup here by `importSettings`, item by item; see
`utils/settingsFile.js`. A file left in the desktop app's data folder by a
script arrives by the same way, as the app opens
(`composables/useSettingsFile.js`).

Until 26 Oct 2026 a project could be saved to a file of its own, and part
of everything as a selection: some projects, documents, chats, cards and
settings. Neither is made any more, and both still come in: a project file
by `readProjectFile`, from the project menu's Import project…, and either
by `readDataFile` as a selection, which `importSelection` adds beside what
is here, merging its settings.

## importProject

Add a project read from a file beside the others.

Everything gets a new id, so the same file can be imported twice, or into
the database it came from, without touching what is there. The rows go
in together or not at all: a project half imported is a tree with no
story, or chats about documents that are not there.

The profiles it runs on come with it, under their own ids. One the
library already holds is used as it stands, as for a chat imported alone:
the library is what the writer has been editing.

The rows are written straight to storage, which the stores read
a project at a time, so they only need telling about the project itself:
its record and its root, which carries its name.

A name given goes on its root before it is written, so the project is
never anything else here — renamed after, its old name came back with
the tree the project opened on, until the rename was saved.

### Parameters

- `project` **ProjectRows**&#x20;
- `options` **[object][2597]?** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `options.title` **[string][2594]?** What to call it, if not what it was called

Returns **[Promise][2599]\<Story>** The project as it now exists here

Blocking an account, from an invitation it sent or from the
people in Settings › Sync and sharing. Every share between the two ends,

## composables/useBulkImport

A batch of files written into the tree, folders and all.

Many files at once — chosen together, a folder chosen whole, or dropped
from the desktop — each looked at and written the way one file is, into
the folders it came in. A folder that is already there under the same name
(in any case) is used; one that is not is made, as `Name (2)` beside a
document of that name. Nothing is asked along the way: a card
in the batch takes the import's defaults, and can be re-imported from its
folder afterwards to answer the questions. One file that cannot be read
is skipped and named at the end, rather than stopping the rest.

## composables/useCardChat

Starting a chat on an imported card.

This is where the pieces meet: the Roleplay profile says how the chat runs,
the card's own documents say who is in it, and the greeting goes in as the
first thing said. None of it is new machinery — a chat stamped from a
profile, what it can see, and a message — which is the point. "Chat with
Seraphina" is a profile being applied, not a feature of cards.

The card's documents open the chat, attached to a turn of the writer's ahead
of the greeting: with the first reply, whether or not the model can read
the project, not read again when a reply is asked again, and kept with the
opening through every summary. See ai/context/attachments.js.

A chat imported from SillyTavern gets here the other way round: it has its
messages already and no idea who it was with beyond a name. `attach` finds
that character's card and puts the same instructions on it.

## composables/useCardImport

A file chosen, looked at, and then written.

Four kinds — a character card in a PNG, a card or a lorebook as JSON, a
markdown document, and a file kept as it is: a PDF, an image, anything —
told apart by what is in them rather than by what they are called. Cards
and lorebooks are read as such only while roleplay is on; otherwise they
are files like any other, and say what they hold. Cards
travel as `.json` as readily as books do, and a PNG is a card only when it
has one in it, so an extension is a hint and not an answer. A Word file is
a markdown document, read out of it as a Google Doc is (`files/docx.js`).

Two steps, for the ones that need it. A card is somebody else's work and
arrives with more in it than its name — a book of several hundred entries, a
dozen greetings, a prompt override — so what it holds is shown before any of
it lands in the writer's tree, and the one question that cannot be asked
afterwards is asked there: whether to take the system prompt. A markdown file has nothing to decide and no surprises in it,
so it is written straight away, and so is a file: its text is read out of it
and it goes where it was asked for.

A card already in the tree can be read back out of its sidecar and written
again over its own folder, with the question asked afresh — `inspectCard`,
and then `write` as for anything else. A card in the writer's library comes
the same way, by `fromLibrary`.

## composables/useChatCommands

Running a slash command against a chat.

The command itself is ai/commands.js and knows nothing about chats. This is
the half that writes the answer into one: a message the writer authored,
carrying the record of what they ran so it can be shown, rerun, and read back
by the context builder.

One speaker per message. The writer rolling an oracle, saying what their
character does, and telling the Director the scene has gone on long enough is
one turn taken in pieces, so it is one message holding those pieces as
segments — they chose to ask, and the answer is established fact by the time
the model reads it. Nothing is inferred and no turn is generated: a command
settles something _before_ there is anything to narrate, which is the whole
point of being able to run three of them and then say one sentence.

The message's own content is the segments assembled — what the model reads,
written once by `assembleTurn` and never by hand. Segments are the writer's
side of it: what they can look at, ask again, and take back out.

A command that consults is the exception, and only because it is not really
one: an interpretation is prose a model wrote, in the same voice everything
else in the assistant slot is written in — a different speaker, so a message
of its own rather than a segment of somebody else's. It holds the answer
alone, and the tag naming what answered goes on in ai/context/build.js on the
way to the wire. What that buys is the thing every other assistant turn
already had: the answer arriving as it is written, rather than a wait with
nothing moving and then a paragraph.

The writer's turn stays one message however it is taken. More written under
a turn pushed in without a reply joins that turn, and two of their messages
left touching when the reply between them goes are folded back into one. It
was always sent as one — see `mergeAdjacentTurns` — and one message is what
lets it be edited, deleted and read as the thing it is. See utils/turns.js.

An aside is never part of a turn. It is a message of its own however the
writer's turn stands, and nothing is folded into it or it into anything,
because the model reads the turns around it and not the aside. See
ai/asides.js. No new ones are made: `/fork` took `/aside`'s place, and the
chat handles it before anything is submitted here.

## submit

Record everything a submission contains, in the order it was written.

Commands all run before anything is written, so a mistyped one leaves the
chat exactly as it was and the writer gets their text back to fix. Once
they have all answered, the segments are written in order — which is the
point of doing it this way at all: a direction belongs after the sentence
it is about, and an oracle after the action it resolves.

What comes back is the prose, for the caller to decide whether there is
anything here to answer — which counts a character's line, since somebody
acting is the turn being taken. A submission of nothing but tools settles
things and asks for no turn.

## fill

Run a command whose message is already in the chat, and fill it in.

A failure is recorded rather than thrown. The message exists and the writer
is looking at it; taking it away to report the failure elsewhere would lose
the question they asked, which is the part worth keeping — they can ask
again from the message itself.

A summary is the exception. It keeps what it had written when it failed
or was stopped, even nothing — the writer may finish it by hand, or start
one and stop it at once to write their own — and nothing on it says it
fell short: an error written into it would be read as part of it. A
failure is reported once it is written, which a stop is not, since the
writer stopped it.

### Parameters

- `messageId` **[string][2594]**&#x20;
- `index` **([number][2595] | null)** Which piece of the turn, or null for a message
  that is nothing but this command
- `parsed` **CommandInput**&#x20;
- `context` **ToolContext**&#x20;

<!---->

- Throws **SummaryCutShortError** When a summary's request failed, once what
  it had written is kept

Returns **[Promise][2599]\<void>**&#x20;

## streamed

## watched

The same context, tied to the record the answer is being written into.

Two things this layer knows and the command does not. The first is where to
put the answer and the thinking: a command with a model behind it gets the
same treatment every other message with a model behind it gets — the writer
watches it think and reads what it made of the draw as it is written, which
is the only view there is of an interpretation's working, since the pair
itself never leaves the skill.

The second is where the question sits. A consultation reads the
conversation as it stood _before_ the message holding it — never itself,
and never, on a second asking, a conversation that has moved on since. An
interpretation made at turn ten is about the story at turn ten however many
times it is asked for. A compaction is the one that reads a little past
itself — it sits above the turns it kept and read them too — but only that
far, so it is about the same conversation however many times it is asked.

  - `$0.messageId` &#x20;
  - `$0.index` &#x20;
  - `$0.parsed` &#x20;

## takeSurvivor

The record this parsed command already has, if it is one that survived.

Identity is the whole line and the answer under it: same command, same
question, same answer. That is what makes it safe where matching questions
up would not be — two identical oracles are told apart by what they said,
and one whose answer the writer changed is not the same record any more.

What it saves is the working. A roll's dice and an interpretation's
thinking cannot be recovered from the text, so a line that came through an
edit untouched keeps them.

The record a line had before its answer was edited: the first left over
with the same command and question. Left where it is, since its answer no
longer matches anything; it is only asked what the answer used to be, so a
roll can tell a changed die from a changed total.

### Parameters

- `spare` &#x20;

Returns **(ChatCommand | [undefined][2602])**&#x20;

## revise

Rewrite a turn, or one piece of it, from the text the writer edited.

The text is the turn: commands as they would be typed, answers written
under them, prose as prose. Anything that came through unchanged keeps the
record it had — including the working, which the text cannot carry — and
anything new is run. A command whose answer the writer wrote or changed is
taken at their word rather than asked again, which is what lets a roll be
fudged and an untouched question stay answered.

## composables/useChatFind

Finding in a chat, most of which is not in the page.

A long chat keeps only the turns near the screen in the page (see
useNearTurns), so the browser's own find cannot see the rest. This finds in
the messages themselves instead: in their text as it reads, the markdown
rendered and its marks gone, so that what is counted is what the writer
would see. Going to a match keeps its turn in the page and scrolls the match
into view.

The matches in the turns that are in the page are highlighted where they
are, with the CSS Custom Highlight API, which marks text without touching
the page: nothing a message renders is rewritten to show a match, and a
message re-rendered under the highlights is simply found in again. Where the
API is missing, a match is still gone to, just not marked.

A message reads as its content, or a turn the writer took in pieces as the
prose of each piece, which is what the chat shows of it. The page has that
text in its `[data-find-text]` elements, inside the element marked with the
message's id. Where the text on screen is not quite the text counted, as in
a message shown raw, the nth match of a message is the nth on screen, or the
last there is.

A typeset formula reads as its glyphs. The MathML KaTeX puts beside them,
for screen readers, is out of sight and so out of the find.

How long after going to a match it is kept in view while the turns around it come in.

## composables/useChatPresets

Giving every chat and profile the model it runs on.

A chat keeps the model it first answered on, and a pick in another chat
moves only what new chats on that profile start on. One from before chats
kept their own models names none, or only the preset it ran on, which is
no longer read: each is given the model it runs on, every chat on this
device once, the first time this version opens, and as a project's chats
load, any that came since from an older device, a backup or an import.

The model is given only where the chat could run on it now. One whose
connection isn't set up yet follows its profile, so setup, which moves the
profiles, moves the chat too.

Profiles are given the model their old preset was on, or where the writer
had chosen a preset for chats before each profile kept its own, that
one's, once, so they start their chats there on every device. Then the
presets that share a connection and model become one (`mergeDuplicates`).

Design: `.llm/ai_setup_design.md`, "Step 1: a chat's model".

## copyChat

Copy a chat's settings and a run of its messages into a new chat in this
story. What a fork and an import have in common.

A copy continues the original conversation, so it carries that chat's
settings over, its own wording, preset, web search and Python among them;
a brand new chat has none of those and reads its profile's. The messages
keep their content and timing and get fresh ids.

What a card put in front of the model comes with the messages: the turn
that opens its chat holds a copy of each document it attached.

What a chat shows and hides is carried: a fork is the same
conversation, and it would be a different one if it could suddenly see
every other character in the project.

### Parameters

- `source` **Chat** Whose settings to carry over
- `messages` **[Array][2596]\<Message>** In order; each is duplicated under the new chat
- `title` **[string][2594]**&#x20;
- `$3` **[Object][2597]** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `$3.now` (optional, default `false`)
  - `$3.named` (optional, default `true`)

Returns **Chat**&#x20;

## forkChat

Fork a chat at a specific message, creating a new chat with all messages up to that point.

A fork taken at an aside carries on from it: the aside is part of the new
chat's conversation, for the writer to say more about. The asides before
it stay on the side, as in any fork. See ai/asides.js.

### Parameters

- `chatId` **[string][2594]** Original chat ID
- `messageId` **[string][2594]** Last message ID to include in the fork

<!---->

- Throws **CannotApplyError** If the chat or the message has gone

Returns **Chat** The newly created forked chat

## importChat

Bring a chat read from a file into this story.

Everything gets a fresh id, so the same file can be imported twice, or
back into the story it came from, without colliding with what is there.

The prompt the chat ran on comes with it. A profile this library already
holds under that id is used as it stands — the file may be older, and the
library is what the writer has been editing. One it does not hold becomes a
profile of the writer's own, made from the file's copy, and the chat runs
on that.

### Parameters

- `chat` **Chat** As it was exported
- `messages` **[Array][2596]\<Message>** Its messages, in order
- `prompt` **AIPrompt?** The prompt it ran on, if the file carried one

Returns **Chat** The chat as it now exists here

## composables/useChatTabs

The chat panel's tabs in a project: which chats are open, in
strip order, which is showing, which is only being looked at, the order
they were shown in, and which the model finished in while they weren't
showing. Kept in the project's view beside the editor's tabs, under the
same rules (`utils/tabs.js`), so a project reopens on its chats.

A chat opened from the chat list is a preview, as a document from the
outline is: the next one takes its tab, until the writer keeps it by
sending in it or double-clicking it. Anything else opens a kept tab beside
the one showing: a new chat, a fork, a chat started on a card. Closing the
tab showing goes back to the one shown before it.

The strip is never empty. With nothing open it shows the unstarted chat,
which is written into the view only once it is used, so opening a chat
from the list then leaves no blank tab behind. There is only ever one
unstarted chat (`useChats`): New chat shows its tab, and its first message
makes it a chat under the same id, in the same tab.

A chat the model stops working in while it isn't the tab showing is
marked unread until it is shown (`useChatActivity`). A turn that stops to
wait for the writer to allow a call has stopped working too.

One instance per project, made in a scope of its own like `useAIChat`, so
the watch that clears what is read outlives the view that first asked.

## composables/useCloudSync

Sync, as the app runs it: signing in and out, and the rounds
that keep this device's projects in step with the writer's others.

Signed in, the device keeps its account in sync's own table: the server's
address, the name, the session's token, and the account's keys as
CryptoKeys that can't be exported, so the passphrase is asked for once.
Every write to a project is noted for sync from then on, in every window.

A file's bytes stay on the server until they are wanted: the files store
fetches them through `cloud/onDemand.js`, which this provides while signed
in.

The writer's setup syncs as well, as the account's own collection
(`cloud/setup.js`): the app tables it is made of reach sync through the
storage facade as a project's rows do, and the settings kept outside the
database are watched here, a group to a row.

Each device gives the server a name for itself (`cloud/deviceName.js`),
so the account's list of devices says which is which, and any of them can
sign another out. A device signed out that way finds out at its next
request, and lets go of what sync kept, as signing out here would.

One window syncs for the app: the one holding the `inksprite-sync` lock.
It listens to the server's stream of changes, and runs a round when one
comes, a few seconds after a write, when the app comes back into view or
online, and every minute. In the desktop app a window also syncs the
projects it holds, and the window syncing for the app tells the others
when the server has something new.

A hosted server may ask a device to wait (too many requests), say the
account is full, or that it was turned off: the rounds wait as long as
asked, the status says the storage is full, and a device turned off stops
syncing and keeps everything, until Sync now finds it on again. Every
quarter of an hour, and as the page is hidden, the device sends the
server what its engine counted (`cloud/diagnostics.js`), unless the writer
turned that off here or the server wants none.

A project can be kept on this device only: its files are fetched here
first, since the server's copy goes, and its story says so (`syncOff`),
which the engine leaves out of every round. Synced again, it goes up whole.

A newer app's records hold the pull until this one is updated, and the
server may refuse an old build's pushes: the app looks for an update at
once, rather than at the next hour (`useUpdates`), and says so once, in a
dialog that offers the update when it is ready (`askedToUpdate`), as well
as in the status line.

A project is shared with friends by their friend codes, from its menu,
whole or only some of its documents, and a friend leaves one shared with
them there. A share reaches them as an invitation, which they accept,
reject, or answer by blocking whoever sent it. The people this account
shares with, and those it blocked, are kept by the server and asked for
here (`people`). Who this account is, who is in each project shared, and
the invitations waiting are kept in `cloud/people.js` for what shows a
comment's author and the invitations; the account's id is kept with it,
so that a comment written before the server is reached says who wrote it too.

Design: `.llm/sync_design.md`.

## composables/useCommandMenu

The menu of commands a slash opens in the message field.

It opens while the caret is in a command's name at the start of a line, and
lists the commands that name could be finishing. It only ever finishes the
name: what comes after is the writer's to type, the same as without it.

## commandOptionId

### Parameters

- `listId` &#x20;
- `name` &#x20;

## commandOptionId

The id of a command's row in the menu, for the row itself and for the
field's `aria-activedescendant`, which names the row a screen reader is on
while the focus stays in the field.

### Parameters

- `listId` **[string][2594]** The menu's id
- `name` **[string][2594]** The command's

Returns **[string][2594]**&#x20;

## useCommandMenu

The menu for one message field.

The field's own keys are the menu's while it is open, and nobody else's:
Enter that would have sent the message finishes the name instead, and Escape
that would have closed the panel closes the menu. So `onKeydown` has to see
a key before the field's own handlers do, which means binding it on
something around the field, in the capture phase; it stops the keys it
uses there. It leaves alone any key it has no use for, and Enter with a
modifier, which already means something else in the field.

Enter is left alone, too, when the name is already typed out in full. The
writer who types `/tarot` and presses Enter wants it sent, not
finished; Tab still finishes it.

Escape shuts it for the rest of that command: typing on does not bring it
back, and it opens again once the caret has left the name and come back to
one. Picking a name shuts it on that name, because a name that takes a
setting is finished without a space, which leaves the caret still in it, and
a menu that opened again there would take the next Enter for itself.

### Parameters

- `field` &#x20;
- `draft` &#x20;

Where the caret is, or null while the field is not focused or holds a selection.

## composables/useComments

The comments in a project, for the list in the sidebar and
the comment under the line: each document that has any, in outline order,
with its open comments where its text has them — the editor's, for a
document open in it, so the list keeps up with typing — its stale ones,
whose passages were deleted, and its resolved ones; and what the writer
does with one: go to it, write it, answer it, change what they said,
resolve it, open it again, and delete it or one of its replies. On the
desktop a new comment is written in the list too, on a passage the editor
holds for it (`commentDraft`), in its place among its document's comments.

A comment is a marker in the text and a thread on the document's row (see
`editor/comments.js`). A thread is placed while its marker is in the text.

A suggestion is listed among them, in the text's order, as Docs lists
them: its thread is on the row too, and its place is the change itself,
marks holding its id (see `editor/suggestions.js`). The writer accepts or
rejects it where a comment is resolved. In a document open in the editor
that is a change to its state, which undoing takes back, and the thread
is open again once its marks are.

What the writer does to a comment or a suggestion is noted, for Mod-Z in
the Comments tab to take back and Shift-Mod-Z to do again, while what it
changed is as it left it (`undo`, `redo`).

Going to a comment makes it the current one, which is app-wide so that the
list and the editor agree on it: the editor scrolls to it and marks it, and
may only take that up once the document it is in has opened. The caret in
a comment in the text makes it current too, and the list shows which.

comment again is asked again: the writer has scrolled away since.

## composables/useConnections

The AI connections the writer has: which are theirs, how each
answered last, and adding, checking and removing one.

A connection is a key or an address: OpenRouter, Anthropic, a server at
home. The writer adds one in setup or in Settings › Connections, and it is
theirs. Every install used to make nine on start, one of each kind
(`BUILT_IN_PROVIDERS`); those still made by older devices, or left from
before, count only while they hold something of the writer's (`isSetUp`).
They are hidden rather than deleted, since an older device would only make
them again.

Each connection's status is its own, and comes from the last real answer:
Connect, or a chat's reply. It is this device's alone, since a server at
home answers one device and not another.

Design: `.llm/ai_setup_design.md`, "Step 2: setup".

## nanoGptRefusal

What NanoGPT's refusal of a model's routing means, by the code it names it
with, where it is one of those; null otherwise. Each is mended by another
model, or by the model's own providers, which the model's fix leads to.

- `zdr_provider_required`: no provider serving it keeps nothing.
- `no_allowed_provider_for_model`, `provider_unknown_provider`: the
  providers chosen for it don't serve it (any more).
- `provider_selection_not_available`, `provider_selected`: a subscription
  with paid models off for its API may not choose providers.

### Parameters

- `code` **unknown**&#x20;
- `provider` **AIProvider**&#x20;
- `model` **[string][2594]**&#x20;

Returns **([string][2594] | null)**&#x20;

## describeFailure

What a reply that failed says, and the fix it offers where there is one: a
refused key or a server not there, its connection; no credits left on
OpenRouter or NanoGPT, more; a model a service no longer offers, or one
NanoGPT can't serve as asked (`nanoGptRefusal`), another. Anything else is
said as the server said it.

Another model, not the connection, where NanoGPT's zero data retention is
what stopped it: it may be the key's own policy, which the connection's
settings can't change.

OpenRouter's 404 is a model it dropped only where no routing step left it
without an endpoint (`routingFilterOf`). Where one did, the connection's
provider routing offers its settings, which the writer may never have
seen, since the floor is on by default; the providers the model is
limited to, or a model that can't use tools, another model.

### Parameters

- `error` **any**&#x20;
- `provider` **(AIProvider | null | [undefined][2602])** What the reply went through
- `model` **[string][2594]**&#x20;

## composables/useCopyLink

Copy a link to a document, or a link in one, to the clipboard.

A link to a document goes as two things at once: a link, its words the
document's name, for the editor and the chat to paste as a link to it, and
its path (`Characters/Elara`, the one address the AI tools take) as plain
text, for anywhere else. Any other link goes as its address. The outline's
menu, the tab strip's, the editor's and its link popover all copy this way.

- `storyId` **[string][2594]**&#x20;

## composables/useDocumentLinks

Links between a project's documents, followed and made.

A link to another document opens it in a tab, as picking it in the outline
does; a link to anywhere else opens outside the app, as before. Following
one is the editor's Mod-click and its link popover, and a click on a link
in a chat. Making one is the link field: a path, a link as it is written,
or the name of a document, becomes the link from the document it goes in.
Copied, a link goes as a path from the top of the project, and pasted it
is written from the document it lands in. See `utils/documentLinks.js`
for how a link is written and read.

## composables/useDocuments

The document tree for one story, shaped for the tree UI.

Thin over `documentsStore`: it scopes everything to a story, owns the
display-title rule, and keeps the folder-vs-text distinction in one place so
components don't each reimplement it.

One instance per storyId, so several mount points (sidebar, mobile) share
state instead of racing to initialise.

It also owns the editor's tabs: which documents are open and which is
showing. They are recorded in the project's view, on this copy of the app,
so the project reopens as it was left, and read back checked against the tree, so a document deleted since
is not among them. `open` and `closeTab` write them; `remove` drops the
tabs of what it deletes, and `keep` makes a preview tab stay. See
`utils/tabs.js` for the rules. A tab can hold a chat's system prompt or
author's note instead of a document, and stays while the chat is there;
see `utils/chatTabs.js`.

It also owns the one rule about where a document's content lives: while a
document is open in the editor, the editor's state is the truth and a write
is a transaction dispatched to it; otherwise the store is. `setContent` and
`appendContent` decide, so that no writer has to know.

Content written here is stored in the file format's own form, the one the
editor serializes. Text from outside — a model's, a file's — may say the
same thing with another bullet or escape, and if the store kept that form
the document would read differently the moment it was opened: a passage an
edit was recorded against would no longer be found, and rewinding would
skip it as if the writer had changed it. A plain document is the
exception: it is never opened as a document, so it is stored as typed.

A rename or a move keeps the project's links going where they went: a link
it leaves going nowhere is written again to where its document is now. See
`utils/linkUpdates.js`.

## uniqueTitle

A title nothing else in this folder already has: `title`, or the first
free one of `Title (2)`, `Title (3)`…

Two rows with one name is a tree the writer cannot read and a path the
model cannot use, so whatever puts a document in a folder without the
writer naming it there — making one, importing one, moving one — takes
the next free name. Importing the same thing twice is a thing people do,
a newer version of it or the same one by accident, and `Elara (2)` says
which came later without pretending to know what changed. A name the
writer types is theirs, and is refused rather than changed: `rename`.

### Parameters

- `parentId` **[string][2594]**&#x20;
- `title` **[string][2594]**&#x20;
- `exceptId` **[string][2594]?** A document moving in, which is not in its own way

Returns **[string][2594]**&#x20;

## composables/useDriveImport

Files picked in Google Drive, brought into a folder of the
project.

The steps are `drive/`'s: Google's sign-in with its picker, in a popup or
the system browser, then each picked file looked up and fetched. This puts
them in order and hands what came back to the bulk importer, as a batch
chosen from disk would be, so a Doc or a Word file is a text document and
a PDF a file document. A Doc is read through the Docs API and converted
(`drive/convert.js`), its pictures fetched and handed on with it; a Doc the
converter is not given comes as Google's markdown export, its pictures
written into it. Either way, as a Word file's, they are its document's own
(see `files/pictures.js`), and those that could not come are counted. A
Doc with suggested edits still open is named, since it comes in as it was
before them, and its first sync brings them in as its comments come in
(`drive/suggestions.js`). A Doc's document is linked to
the Doc (`drive`): its id, its tab, and the account that picked it, for
syncing the two later, and the sign-in is kept for the syncs after it
(`drive/session.js`). See `.llm/google_docs_design.md`.

## composables/useDriveSync

A linked document synced with its Google Doc, from its menu
or the Sync button over it.

The steps are `drive/sync.js`'s. This signs in for them (`drive/session.js`,
from the click, which in a browser is what lets Google's window open),
hands them the document as it stands and its base, and puts what comes
back in place: the Doc's new pictures made the document's own, the
document edited to the merge rather than replaced, so a document open
keeps its caret and can undo the sync in one step, the Doc's text kept as
a version where words of it gave way to the document's, and the Doc as it
now reads kept as the next sync's base.

A text document not linked to a Doc can be synced to a new one: a Doc
made under its title in the writer's Drive, in the account the project
last synced with, linked, and the document synced into it. A Doc made so
is kept in `inksprite-sync`, in folders as the project has them
(`drive/folders.js`), moved and renamed at each sync to match.

The Doc's suggested edits come in as suggestions, and are accepted or
rejected in it when they are here (`drive/suggestions.js`); the model's
go to the Doc as suggestions in the writer's name, as its comments do.

Design: `.llm/google_docs_design.md`, part 3, Sync.

## composables/useEditor

The open documents. One entry per document open in the editor,
app-wide, kept for as long as the document is open.

A structured document opens as an `EditorState`, and while it is open that
state is the truth: every change — a keystroke, an AI append, an undo — is
a transaction dispatched here. A plain document opens as its text, and the
text is the truth: what is typed replaces it, and an outside write lands on
it as it is, never settled. Either way the store's copy is a projection,
serialized on a debounce, on blur, on close, and on `flush()`. `flush()`
with no id writes out every open document, and is called before anything
reads the store expecting the latest text, the way a backup is taken.
Closed, the store's markdown is the truth and writes go there. There is
never a moment when both are authoritative for the same document.

`useDocuments` owns the routing between the two: a writer that wants to
change a document asks it, and it asks here only when the document is open.
Nothing else should. `Editor.vue` puts a view in front of a structured
document's state and hands transactions back through `dispatch`;
`RawMarkdown.vue` puts a field in front of a plain document's text and
hands what is typed back through `setText`. The registry is reactive to
that extent: a computed over `markdown(id)` follows the document as it
changes.

## Entry

Type: (DocumentEntry | TextEntry)

### Properties

- `kind` **`"document"`**&#x20;
- `state` **EditorState**&#x20;
- `view` **(View | null)** The view showing the state, if one is
- `dirty` **[boolean][2600]** Changed since the store last heard
- `scrollTop` **[number][2595]** Where the view was scrolled to when it last wentA plain document, open: its text, as typed.
- `kind` **`"text"`**&#x20;
- `text` **[string][2594]**&#x20;
- `dirty` **[boolean][2600]**&#x20;
- `scrollTop` **[number][2595]**&#x20;
- `anchor` **unknown** Where its view was scrolled to, as that view
  keeps it: a long text's view guesses at the height of what it has not
  drawn, so a pixel offset does not come back to the same line

## composables/useFocusMode

Focus mode: the document alone, filling the screen.

Everything but the page goes: the rail, the sidebar, the chat, the strip
of tabs, and on a phone the tab bar. The page goes full screen as well,
where it can be: in a browser that lets it, and in the desktop app.

Option-Command-F, or Control-Alt-F off a Mac, goes in and comes out, as
Scrivener's composition mode does. Escape comes out too, once nothing
else on the page has taken it, and so does leaving full screen whichever
way the writer leaves it. A browser full screen keeps Escape for itself,
so the find would stay open behind it; Chrome, Edge and the desktop app
let the page have it, and leave full screen on Escape held down instead.

One state for the app: the writer's frame lays itself out by it, and the
editor panel drops its tabs.

## focused

Whether the writer is in focus mode.

## ownFullScreen

Whether focus mode put the page in full screen, and so takes it out again.
A page already full screen when focus mode began is left as it was.

## isFocusKey

Whether a key is the one for focus mode: Option-Command-F on a Mac,
Control-Alt-F elsewhere.

Option changes the character a Mac reports, so there the key is also known
by where it is. Off a Mac it has to be an F: AltGr is Control-Alt to a
browser there, and on some keyboards types a character with that key.

### Parameters

- `event` **[KeyboardEvent][2612]**&#x20;

Returns **[boolean][2600]**&#x20;

## keyboard

The keyboard lock, which gives the page keys the browser would keep while it
is full screen. Chromium's alone, and not in the DOM's types yet.

Go full screen, unless the page is already or cannot be.

keeps the key for itself, or the window's own button, leaves focus mode.

## isFocusEscape

Whether an Escape that reached the page is focus mode's. The editor marks
every Escape handled, so being handled says nothing; what has a use for
one stops it on the way instead: the find, and a link or comment being
written. A menu or a dialog closes on it, and focus mode stays.

## composables/useGenerationSettings

Read and write a model's generation settings on a connection:
sampler parameters, seed, max tokens, how the model's reasoning shows, and
how many tool rounds a turn may take.

Three layers: the app's defaults, then the samplers the model's makers say
it runs best at (its list's `defaults`), then the writer's changes, kept
sparsely: a key is present only once the writer has changed it, so an
untouched one keeps up with the layers below. The model's settings are
made the first time one is changed (`changeModelSettings` in useAIConfig).
`effective` is what a request would actually use.

## composables/useHoverSubmenus

A TieredMenu's submenus opening as the pointer reaches them.

PrimeVue's TieredMenu opens a submenu on a click, and on hover only after
one has been opened that way. It remembers that in its `dirty` flag and
forgets it as the menu closes, with no option for starting without it, so
the flag is kept set here.

Two more things then go wrong, and are put right through the menu's
pass-through, which reaches each item:

- A submenu goes the moment the pointer is on another item, and a straight
  line to something low in a submenu crosses the items under the one it
  opened from. So the menu hears of a pointer on an item only once it has
  rested there.
- A click on an item shuts its submenu if it is open, and now the pointer
  has opened it on the way to the click. A click from habit would see it go,
  so that click is stopped short of the menu.

A finger has no hover. A tap sends the mouse events and then the click, so
where the main pointer cannot hover the menu is left as it is. In a narrow
window a submenu opens inline and the menu goes by clicks alone, so there a
click still shuts it.

## REST

How long the pointer rests on an item before the menu hears of it, in ms.

Type: [number][2595]

## INLINE

TieredMenu's default breakpoint, under which its submenus open inline.

Type: [string][2594]

## keepsOpen

What an item with its submenu open does with a click: nothing.

### onClickCapture

#### Parameters

- `event` **[Event][2611]**&#x20;

- `menu` &#x20;

Returns **[Object][2597]** Pass-through for the menu to take

## composables/useJumpToBottom

When to offer a way back to the end of a long scroll.

A chat does not follow its newest message down — see Chat.vue — so a writer
who has gone back up through a long one has a long way to come back. The
button that takes them there is offered when two things are true at once:

- the end is far away, more than a panel's height below what they can see.
  Any nearer and the scroll wheel is as quick, and a button over the text is
  in the way;
- they are heading for it. Somebody scrolling up is going back to read
  something, and a button that appears under their pointer as they do is
  offering to undo what they are in the middle of. Scrolling down is the
  moment the offer is an answer to anything.

Only the writer's own scrolling counts as heading anywhere. The chat moves
the panel itself — to the top of a summary as it starts being written, to the
end of the chat when something is sent or one is opened — and says so with
`hush`, so that its own movement is not read as somebody's intent.

How far is far is one answer, and the chat asks it too: a writer that far
from the end has gone to read something, and is not brought back by a
message landing there.

## HUSH_MS

How long after the chat moves the panel its scrolling is taken to be the chat's.

Type: [number][2595]

## MAX_PASSES

How many times a jump goes again when the end moved under it.

Type: [number][2595]

## drawn

Once the next frame has been laid out and drawn.

## useJumpToBottom

### Parameters

- `scroller` &#x20;
- `spare` (optional, default `ref(0)`)

How far below what can be seen the end of the content is.

### Parameters

- `panel` **[HTMLElement][2616]**&#x20;

## far

Whether the end is more than a panel's height below what can be seen.

## onScroll

The panel scrolled. Wired to its `scroll` event.

## hush

The chat is about to move the panel itself.

## jump

Go to the end of the content, at once rather than smoothly, as other chat
apps do. Turns off screen stand at a guessed height until they are laid
out, so the end moves as the ones passed on the way come into view: a
smooth scroll to where the end was when it set out stopped short of where
it is. The panel can change height under it too, as the message box sizes
itself when a chat opens. So the jump is made again once a frame has been
drawn, until it is at the end.

Returns **[Promise][2599]\<void>**&#x20;

## composables/useKeyboardCover

How much of an element the on-screen keyboard covers.

Android makes the page smaller when the keyboard comes up (the viewport's
`interactive-widget=resizes-content`), so nothing is covered there. iOS
leaves the page the size of the screen and shows less of it, so the bottom
of a full-height element sits behind the keyboard: what is visible is the
visual viewport, which this measures against.

## useKeyboardCover

How many pixels at the bottom of the element are behind the keyboard, kept
up as the keyboard comes and goes and the page is panned under it.

### Parameters

- `element` &#x20;

## composables/useLongPress

A finger held still on something, for what a right-click opens
everywhere else.

A phone has no right-click, and iOS fires no `contextmenu` for a long press,
so the press is timed here. It is a press only while the finger stays put: a
finger that moves first is scrolling, and is left to.

A finger that moves once the press has been taken is dragging what it is on,
which a held finger also starts in the outline, so whatever the press opened
is told to close again. A finger lifted after a press is not a tap: the
click that would follow is cancelled, so the row it was on does not open as
the menu does.

## LONG_PRESS_MS

How long a finger has to stay down to be a long press. iOS takes about this long.

Type: [number][2595]

## SLOP

How far a finger can wander, in pixels, and still be held still.

Type: [number][2595]

## composables/useMcpServers

The writer's MCP servers: adding one, listing what it offers
again, and the tools they always allow. Which chats use one is each chat's,
among its tools (ai/tools/choice.js).

Adding is two steps, because what a server offers is what the model will be
told: `preview` connects and lists its tools with their descriptions for the
writer to read, and `addServer` keeps it. A server that runs as a local
program is kept without a preview, and shown as needing a bridge.

A server that wants the writer to sign in says so when it is previewed or
listed, and `signIn` sends them, in a tab of its own, to its authorization
server; the tab comes back to `/connect/mcp`, which finishes it and says so
on a channel this listens to. See mcp/auth.js. In the desktop window the
sign-in opens in the system browser instead, and comes back to the window,
which finishes it itself (`platform/signIn.js`).

## ServerPreview

What a server offers, read for the writer before it is kept.

- `instructions` **[string][2594]** What it tells a client about using it
- `tools` **[Array][2596]\<Omit\<McpTool, `"exposed"`>>**&#x20;
- `prompts` **[Array][2596]\<McpPrompt>**&#x20;

## SIGN_IN_WAIT_MS

How long a sign-in tab is waited on before the writer is told to try again.

## signIns

Counts every sign-in and sign-out in this tab, or announced by another, so
whatever shows whether a server is signed in reads it again. The sign-ins
themselves are kept in local storage, which nothing is told about.

## composables/useMessageField

Keep the chat's message field fitted to the draft it holds.

## fitsBeside

Whether the draft fits on the one line its buttons leave beside it.

Measured by laying the row out that way for a moment — nothing wrapping,
the field at the width beside the buttons and at its one-row height — and
asking whether the draft overflows it. It is measured at that width however
the row is laid out at the time, because that is the only width the answer
is stable at: a draft that just fills one line on its own would fit beside
the buttons on two, and measured where it was it would say something
different every frame.

Heights are whole pixels and a line of text need not be, so one line can
measure a pixel over its own box. Another line is a lot more than that.

### Parameters

- `row` **[HTMLElement][2616]** The flex row the field shares with its buttons
- `field` **[HTMLElement][2616]** The textarea

Returns **[boolean][2600]**&#x20;

## useMessageField

Keep a message field fitted to its draft: as tall as the draft needs, up to
the cap its class sets, and beside its buttons only while the draft fits
there on one line. Past that the field takes the whole row and the buttons
drop under it, so a paragraph is not written in the column a row of buttons
leaves.

The field is borderless, and sized here rather than by auto-resize: both
follow from scrollHeight leaving borders out. A bordered field is set two
pixels short of its own content and sits permanently scrolled; a borderless
one is set exactly, which is the one case auto-resize can never shrink again.

### Parameters

- `field` &#x20;
- `row` &#x20;
- `draft` &#x20;

## fit

Size the field to the draft, past the cap of which the rest of the draft
is behind a scrollbar.

## composables/useNarration

A project read aloud, one document at a time.

Over the stores and the `tts` module: the project's voices, hints and
filters, and the connection and model it is read through, read off the
story and written back to it; a document's speakers, read off the document
and written back; and the readings themselves, which live here. In the
desktop app's library each clip is kept with the project too, and read
back when the document is next read aloud (`restore`); in a browser a
reading is a session's worth of audio, cheap to make again on Kokoro and
too big to keep.

One instance per story, so the panel and anything else that asks share
the readings in progress rather than starting their own.

A reading keeps its audio by what was said and in whose voice (see
`tts/reading.js`), so it can be made a piece at a time: the whole
document, some blocks, one block again. Asked for the document, it
reads only what has no audio yet. Whatever there is audio for is joined
into one track, in document order, when a run ends and whenever the
document stops agreeing with the track it has; stopping halfway leaves
something to hear.

## ReadingTrack

The audio a document has, joined: where each block plays.

Type: [Object][2597]

### Properties

- `segments` **[Array][2596]<{start: [number][2595], end: [number][2595], index: [number][2595]}>** In seconds, with the block each is
- `duration` **[number][2595]** Seconds
- `key` **[string][2594]** What it was joined from; see `trackKeyOf`

## Reading

A document's reading: the audio it has, and how the last run went.

Type: [Object][2597]

### Properties

- `status` **(`"idle"` | `"running"` | `"done"` | `"stopped"` | `"failed"`)** The last run, or the one under way
- `done` **[number][2595]** How many utterances this run has read
- `total` **[number][2595]** How many it set out to
- `current` **([string][2594] | null)** The signature being asked for now
- `failed` **([string][2594] | null)** The signature the last run failed on
- `error` **([string][2594] | null)** Why it failed, when it did
- `clips` **[Map][2598]<[string][2594], [ArrayBuffer][2604]>** The audio, by signature. Reactive.
- `track` **([ReadingTrack][1929] | null)** The audio joined, in document order
- `url` **([string][2594] | null)** The track as an object URL, for a player

first time; after an edit, only what changed — and when nothing lacks

way, this does nothing.
